chartPlan.howToRead: Note the 1.9 national line versus the 2.1 threshold.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Assuming urban fertility drives the national average; rural is much larger.

chartPlan.title: India's fertility in a global context
chartPlan.whyShowThis: India's fall is not unique: it has joined the low-fertility world, but sits above every advanced economy and far above East Asia's ultra-low rates.
chartPlan.howToRead: Compare India's line with peers; it's converging but still higher.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Thinking India's rate is exceptionally low; many countries are much lower.

chartPlan.title: Fertility by state
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Fertility is not one number; it is a north-south map.
chartPlan.howToRead: Look at the colour gradient; darkest in north-central India.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Assuming uniform progress across all states.

chartPlan.title: Highest and lowest fertility states
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The map, sharpened into a league table.
chartPlan.howToRead: Scan the top and bottom five values.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Ignoring population weights; small states can have extreme values.

chartPlan.title: At what age Indian women have children
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Fertility is not just how many, but when.
chartPlan.howToRead: Spot the peak at 25-29 (134.7) and the steep drop after 34.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Thinking teen births are common; they are low per 1,000.

chartPlan.title: Women are having children later
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Are women delaying childbirth? The trend says yes.
chartPlan.howToRead: See the line rise from 25.48 to 30.49.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Assuming mean age rising means fewer children; it also compresses childbearing.

chartPlan.title: How India avoids pregnancy, and who carries it
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Falling fertility runs on contraception, and in India that burden is overwhelmingly female.
chartPlan.howToRead: Compare female sterilisation bar to male sterilisation.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Thinking all contraception is modern; permanent methods dominate.

chartPlan.title: Families are getting smaller
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Smaller families are the texture of below-replacement fertility.
chartPlan.howToRead: Majority of births are first children (66.4%); fourth+ only 3.5%.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Forgetting that this is share, not absolute numbers.

chartPlan.title: Marrying and giving birth young
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Early marriage and teenage motherhood still shape fertility at the margins.
chartPlan.howToRead: Note the percentages and compare with earlier rounds if known.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Assuming these figures are only about fertility; they reflect gender norms.

chartPlan.title: Fertility falls with schooling
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Education is the strongest single lever on fertility.
chartPlan.howToRead: See the steady drop from 2.82 to 1.78 as schooling increases.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Thinking education is the sole cause; it correlates with many changes.

chartPlan.title: Fertility falls with wealth
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Fertility is also a class story.
chartPlan.howToRead: Look at the gradient from lowest quintile (2.63) to highest (1.57).
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Assuming wealth causes low fertility; both are part of development.

chartPlan.title: Fertility by religion
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The most misread fertility number in India, shown plainly.
chartPlan.howToRead: Compare groups, but note the convergence context.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Interpreting differences as permanent or driven by religion alone.

chartPlan.title: Boys per girl at birth: the son-preference signal
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Fewer children combined with a preference for sons shows up as too few girls born.
chartPlan.howToRead: Check all-India line at 918, and note rural vs urban gap.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Thinking 918 is close to natural ratio; it indicates missing girls.

chartPlan.title: India's age pyramid today
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Who those people are, by age and sex.
chartPlan.howToRead: Look at the wide base (youth) and the narrow top (elderly).
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Forgetting this is a snapshot; the pyramid shape evolves.

chartPlan.title: The age mix is shifting
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Ageing is three shares moving at once.
chartPlan.howToRead: Watch the children share fall, working-age rise, then plateau, and elderly rise.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Thinking working-age share will stay high; it will eventually decline.

chartPlan.title: Median age, to 2100
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The single number for how old the country is.
chartPlan.howToRead: See the projection from today's young age to near 48 by 2100.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Confusing median with life expectancy.

chartPlan.title: Old-age dependency ratio
chartPlan.whyShowThis: How many older adults each 100 working-age adults support.
chartPlan.howToRead: Look at the upward trend beyond 2030.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Assuming all working-age adults are employed.

chartPlan.title: Indians are living longer
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The other engine of ageing: longer lives, not just fewer births.
chartPlan.howToRead: See the rise from 45.61 to 72.24 years.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Confusing life expectancy with median age.

chartPlan.title: Share of Indians aged 65 and over
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The clearest sign of ageing.
chartPlan.howToRead: Note the current 7.1% and the steep projected rise.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Thinking 7% is small; it doubles quickly in demographic transitions.

chartPlan.title: Income per person as India ages
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The 'old before rich' question: how wealthy India is as it greys.
chartPlan.howToRead: See GDP per capita at $2,695 today, but remember context.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Using GDP per capita as typical income; it's an average.

chartPlan.title: India's population to 2100: the peak
chartPlan.whyShowThis: The payoff: when India stops growing and starts to shrink.
chartPlan.howToRead: Look for the peak around 2061, then gradual decline.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Assuming the peak is guaranteed; it depends on fertility assumptions.

chartPlan.title: How high, how soon? Scenarios to 2100
chartPlan.whyShowThis: How much the future hinges on fertility.
chartPlan.howToRead: See the fan of lines; low fertility leads to much smaller population.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Treating any single scenario as the true future.

chartPlan.title: The models disagree on the peak
chartPlan.whyShowThis: How confident can we be about the peak? Compare the two most-cited models.
chartPlan.howToRead: Note UN median vs IHME reference; IHME peaks earlier and lower.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Thinking models are facts; they are informed guesses.

visualizationDecisions.reason: Full historical arc shows the magnitude and steepness of growth.
Long decline is the key story; annual points reveal the pace.
Peak and decline need the full projection to 2100.
Recent SRS data best shown as a short series to highlight latest levels.
Ranking states works best as horizontal bar chart, mobile-friendly.
Age-specific rates are a single-year snapshot; bars clearly show the peak.
Pyramid is the standard, intuitive visualization for age-sex structure.
Three lines on one axis show the shifting composition over time.
Continuous line shows the steady ageing process.
Ratio over time is best as a line; use the most common measure (65+/15-64).

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The average number of children a woman would have over her lifetime if she experienced current birth rates at each age. It is a snapshot of fertility in a given year, not how many children any real woman has.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: TFR is the key number driving India's population future; below 2.1 means eventually, the population will stop growing without migration.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: About 2.1 children per woman, the level at which each generation exactly replaces itself in the long run, accounting for some children not surviving. Below 2.1, each generation is smaller than the last.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India's TFR at 1.9 (SRS 2024) means it has fallen below replacement, signalling eventual population decline, though momentum delays it.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The tendency for a population to keep growing for decades even after fertility drops, because many young people are still entering childbearing age. Like a heavy train that keeps rolling after the engine is cut.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India's growth today is mainly momentum from earlier high fertility, not current birth rates.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The age that divides the population into two equal halves: half are younger, half are older. It is a measure of how old a population is overall.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India's median age is rising from 21 to nearly 48 by 2100 (UN median), showing rapid ageing.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The number of people aged 65 and older per 100 people of working age (15-64). It gives a rough sense of the economic burden of supporting the elderly.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: As India ages, this ratio will rise sharply, putting pressure on families and social systems.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Total economic output (goods and services) of a country divided by its population, in current US dollars. It's an average, so it doesn't reflect how much a typical person earns.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India is ageing with a GDP per capita around $2,700, far lower than rich countries when they aged, raising the 'old before rich' concern.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The number of live births in a year per 1,000 people in the total population. It is 'crude' because it doesn't account for whether the population is young or old.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Used to show raw birth flow; India's SRS 2024 rate is 18.3.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The average number of years a newborn would live if current death rates stayed the same throughout their life. It summarizes mortality conditions.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Rising life expectancy (from 46 to 72) means more Indians reaching old age, accelerating ageing.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The number of girls born per 1,000 boys. A natural ratio is around 950-970 girls per 1,000 boys; lower numbers indicate missing girls, often due to sex-selective practices.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India's ratio of 918 (SRS 2022-24) signals persistent son preference, though it has improved.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The average age at which women give birth, weighted by age-specific fertility rates. A rising mean age means women are having children later in life.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India's mean age rose from 25.5 to 30.5 (UN projection), indicating delayed childbearing which lowers fertility.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A calculation of what the population would be in the future based on assumptions about fertility, mortality, and migration. It is not a prediction; different assumptions produce different projections.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: All future population figures are projections, and the range of outcomes shows we cannot be certain about the exact peak.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: An official count of every person in the country, usually done every 10 years. It provides the most accurate population figure.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India's last census was in 2011; all current total population numbers are estimates, not counts. The 2024 census is underway.

selectionRules: Start from the page question, not from the indicator name.
Choose the smallest set of visuals that explains scale, trend, structure, comparison, and caveat.
Prefer mobile-friendly charts: line charts with sparse ticks, horizontal bars, share strips, pyramids only when essential, and no dense tables.
Use one strong pull quote only when the evidence supports it with a number.
Add glossary blocks for technical terms that normal readers may not know.
caveats: Use only figures present in lockedNumbers or sourceSummaries.
If a related theme indicator is present, you may use it for context, but do not pretend it is the main answer.
If source coverage is thin, say so directly.
Do not compare states, districts, or cities unless the evidence packet contains those geographies.
forbiddenClaims: Do not infer causality from a trend unless the evidence explicitly supports it.
Do not cite a source that is not present in sourceSummaries.
